name: Interview behavioural questions, set 2
description: Spoken behavioural questions with models and rubrics: leading, learning, market makers, standing out, setbacks, plain words, known puzzles. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Describe a time you led a group without being in charge of it.
widget.model: I led a five-person society team in my second year without being its captain. We were building an entry for a stock-pitch contest. Two weeks before the deadline we had three half-finished models and no shared plan. I offered to draft a timeline rather than take over. I listed every task, put an owner and a date by each, and asked the group to change anything. Two people swapped tasks, which helped. I also set up a fifteen-minute check-in every other evening. When one model kept slipping, I paired with its owner for an hour instead of rewriting it myself. We submitted a day early and placed third of 24 teams. The judges praised how consistent our numbers were across sections. I learned that leading without a title means making the plan visible and letting people own their part. Now I offer a draft first, because people find a draft easier to improve than to start.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: a group you led without the title
A specific situation: the group, the deadline and what was going wrong
Your own actions in the first person, including how you brought others with you
A number or concrete result, such as a placing or time saved
A lesson about leading without authority, stated plainly
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer shows influence without a title: you made the work easier, and the group chose to follow. Name your own actions and how you brought others along. End with the result and what you would repeat.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to learn something hard, quickly.
widget.model: Last summer I had ten days to learn enough SQL to rebuild a monthly report for a small charity. I had only used spreadsheets, and the old report took a volunteer two days each month. I made a plan: three days on the basics, then straight into the real tables. Each morning I did one short course module. Each afternoon I tried to answer one real question with it. When I got stuck, I wrote down the exact error before asking the charity's developer. That way I asked one precise question instead of a vague one. By day eight my query matched the old report on every figure for three past months. The report now runs in about ten minutes instead of two days. The lesson for me was to learn on the real problem as early as possible. Tutorials taught me the syntax, but the real tables taught me what mattered.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: what you had to learn and how fast
A specific situation: why it was hard and what was at stake
Your own learning plan in the first person, and how you got unstuck
A number or concrete result that shows you learned it
A lesson about how you learn, stated plainly
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer names something hard and the deadline, then shows your method for learning it. Interviewers listen for how you got unstuck and how you checked you were right. A result with a number shows the learning worked.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Why do you want to work at a market maker rather than a hedge fund?
widget.model: I want a market maker because I like making many small, quick decisions and learning from each one. A market maker quotes prices all day and earns a small edge on a very large number of trades. A hedge fund usually takes fewer, larger positions and holds them for weeks or months. Both are interesting, but the feedback is very different. At a market maker I would know within hours whether my pricing was good. My evidence is a summer coding project. I wrote a small quoting program for a simulated exchange, and it traded about 2,000 times a day. I spent most evenings tuning it from the day's fills, and that was the part I enjoyed most. So I want fast feedback, a focus on pricing, and training on the firm's own capital.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence with a reason, not "I like markets"
Shows what a market maker does day to day
Contrasts fairly with a hedge fund, without running it down
Evidence from your own experience, with a number
Links the reasons back to this kind of firm
Under two minutes, clear, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer shows how the two businesses differ: many small trades against fewer, larger positions. Give a reason that fits you, backed by evidence with a number. Treat the other path fairly.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: You have thirty seconds to prepare and two minutes to answer. What makes you stand out from other applicants?
widget.model: What makes me stand out is that I test my own ideas against data before I trust them. Most applicants will have good grades and some coding, so I will give one example. In my second year I believed a simple momentum rule beat holding a share index. Before telling anyone, I wrote a backtest over fifteen years of daily prices. It looked strong until I added trading costs of five basis points a trade. Then the edge fell from four per cent a year to almost nothing. I wrote up the result anyway, with the cost check, and shared it with my study group. Two of them now run the same check on their own projects. So my difference is a habit: I look first for the reason I might be wrong. In a trading role, that habit protects capital.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence with one quality, not a list
Backs it with one concrete example: when and what
Your own actions in the first person
A number or result from the example
Links the quality to the role
Fits two minutes after thirty seconds of thought, with a clear end

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: On a recorded answer nobody can ask a follow-up, so pick one quality and one example. Say the quality in your first sentence and back it with numbers. Close by linking it to the job.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a rejection or a setback, and what you did next.
widget.model: Last year a trading firm turned me down after its final round, and it changed how I prepare. I had passed the online test and two interviews, so I expected an offer. The feedback said my mental maths was accurate but slow under pressure. I was disappointed, and I took a weekend off. Then I made a plan. I did twenty minutes of timed arithmetic every morning for eight weeks and logged my speed. Twice a week I also practised market-making games aloud with a friend, so I got used to being interrupted. My average time on a two-digit product fell from about nine seconds to under five. This year I have passed two online tests and reached a final round again. The lesson was that a rejection with feedback is a training plan. Now I ask for feedback every time, even after a success.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: a real rejection or setback, owned plainly
A specific situation, with the feedback or the cause
What you did next, in the first person, as a plan
A number or concrete result that shows the change
A lesson or habit you kept, stated plainly
About two minutes, with no blame of the firm or anyone else

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer is honest about the setback and brief about the disappointment. Most of the time goes on what you did next, with a number that shows it worked. End with the habit you kept.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Explain one technical project to someone who is not a specialist. You have two minutes.
widget.model: I built a program that predicts how long a bus takes to reach its next stop. It helps an app show better arrival times. Think of it as a weather forecast for one short journey. The old app used a fixed time for each stretch of road, which was badly wrong at rush hour. My program learned from a year of past journeys. It saw how the time changes with the hour, the day and the weather. One choice mattered most. I could have used a complex model, but I chose a simpler one that people could check. When it was wrong, we could see why. On three months of journeys kept back for testing, the average error fell from four minutes to under two. The app team now uses it on two routes. If I did it again, I would talk to drivers first, because they knew things the data did not.

rubric.text: Says what the project does in one plain sentence, with no jargon
Uses an everyday comparison the listener already knows
One decision you made, with the alternative you rejected and why
Numbers for the result, in units the listener understands
What you would do differently
Within two minutes, with no unexplained technical term

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong plain account says what the project does before how it works. Use one comparison the listener knows, one decision with its reason, and a result in plain units. Explain every technical word you keep.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: The interviewer gives you a puzzle you have seen before. What do you say?
widget.model: I would say so straight away: "I have seen this one before, so I may remember the answer." Hiding it is risky. A fast answer with no working looks rehearsed, and the interviewer will often know. Then I would offer a choice. I can solve it aloud from scratch, showing the method rather than the answer I remember. Or they can give me a different puzzle. If they want me to go on, I would restate the problem and check its conditions. Then I would work it through step by step, saying why each step holds. I would also try one edge case or a small variant. That shows I understand it rather than recall it. Being open costs me nothing. A good interviewer cares how I think, and honesty is part of what they are hiring.

rubric.text: Says at once, plainly, that you have seen the puzzle before
Explains why honesty matters here: trust, and an answer that looks rehearsed
Offers a choice: solve it aloud from first principles or take a new one
If going on, shows the method step by step, not only the answer
Checks an edge case or a variant, so the reasoning is seen to transfer
Calm, short and in order, without long silences

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Interviewers value honesty over a rehearsed answer, and they often know when a puzzle is familiar. Say so at once and offer to solve it aloud or take another. If you go on, show the method and check an edge case.
